name: Pine Wind Fingering (Tùng Phong Chỉ Pháp)
concept: The outer gate's method. A student sits in the ravine with an unstrung zither and learns to hear the wind in the pines as eight pitches, then strings it and plays them back. Qi is drawn in on the breath with each plucked note and settles in the fingertips. It runs on no element: a Metal child's notes ring and a Wood child's notes hum, and the method does not care which.
lore: The founder's listeners wrote it down in 621 in the zither tablature the academy still uses, the year after the monk left them his zither (C130).

name: Ten Thousand Ravines Zither Canon (Vạn Hác Cầm Kinh)
concept: The academy's canon: one long piece in twelve movements, each a layer, played until it sounds like wind in ten thousand ravines. The player's qi goes out with the sound and comes back from every wall of the ravine, and what returns is drawn in. In a fight it is a song cultivator's method: lulling, marching and cutting notes that stack a Resonance on everything that hears them, and a final movement that sets every Resonance ringing at once.
lore: Played first by the monk under the pines in 620 (C130) and written down by his listeners in tablature. The twelfth movement takes a whole night to play; Hà Thính Tùng is the only living person who has played it to the end.

name: The Monk's Rest (Tăng Hưu Khúc)

effects.name: The Earned Rest
effects.rule: When your Marching Dirge finale ends a march, The Held Rest starts at once and lasts 0.5 s for each Measure the finale spent instead of 2 s, and each later finale's rest this fight is half as long as the one before; while it holds, the foe carries one Heavy Breath stack (its arts cost 25 % more).

concept: The rest between notes, studied as a piece of its own. The holder stops playing, and the silence that follows is so complete that a foe's arts falter in it: their casting slows and their next art may fail. It is taught to inner disciples after they can play the canon's third movement, because silence must be earned by sound.
lore: Named for the monk who left the zither in 620 and walked back to his temple. The academy says he taught only one thing, which was when to stop.
